Key words

Glossary

Words you may hear at appointments or read on this website, explained simply.

Initial glossary being validated by the clinical team and the UPC Language and Terminology Service. Catalan is the source language.

  • A
  • B
  • C
  • D
  • E
  • F
  • G
  • H
  • I
  • L
  • M
  • O
  • P
  • R
  • S
  • V
  • W

A

AMD (age-related macular degeneration)
An age-related disease of the macula, the central part of the retina. It affects central vision (reading, recognising faces), while peripheral vision is usually preserved.
Assistive technology for sight loss
Techniques, devices and software that make technology usable for people with sight loss: screen readers and magnifiers, braille displays, electronic magnifiers and so on (known in Spanish and Catalan as 'tiflotecnología').

B

Braille display
A device connected to a computer or phone that shows on-screen text in braille, using pins that move up and down. Used mainly by people who are blind or have very little sight.

C

Charles Bonnet syndrome
Seeing things that are not there (shapes, patterns, people or landscapes) in people with significant sight loss. It is not a mental illness: it is the brain's response to missing visual input. It is worth mentioning to the eye-care professional.
Co-creation
Designing a resource or service together with the people who will use it. In this project, people with low vision, professionals and organisations take part.
Contrast sensitivity
The ability to tell an object from its background when the difference in brightness is small. It matters a great deal in daily life: seeing steps, faces or text on grey paper.

D

Diabetic retinopathy
Damage to the blood vessels of the retina caused by diabetes. Regular eye examinations and good diabetes control help prevent it from progressing.

E

Easy read
A way of writing and presenting text so that more people can understand it: short sentences, everyday words and ideas in a clear order.
Eccentric viewing
A technique of looking slightly to one side so that a healthy area of the retina, outside the damaged centre, is used. It is learned in visual rehabilitation.
Electronic magnifier
A device with a camera and screen that enlarges text and objects and lets you change colours and contrast. There are portable and desktop models (video magnifiers or CCTVs).

F

Filter lenses
A tinted lens that blocks part of the light (often short-wavelength light) to reduce glare and improve perceived contrast.

G

Glare
Discomfort or loss of vision caused by too much light or by reflections. It is very common in low vision and can be reduced with filters, a visor or cap, and good lighting.
Glaucoma
A group of diseases that damage the optic nerve, often associated with raised eye pressure. It usually affects peripheral vision first and has no symptoms at the start, which is why regular check-ups matter.

H

High (pathological) myopia
Very high short-sightedness (usually over 6 dioptres) that may be accompanied by damage to the retina and macula, retinal detachment or glaucoma.

I

Intraocular lens
An artificial lens placed inside the eye, usually during cataract surgery, to replace the natural lens.

L

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)
A rare inherited disease that damages the optic nerve and causes rapid loss of central vision, often in young people. Side vision is usually partly preserved.
Legal blindness
When vision is below limits set by law or by an organisation (for ONCE membership in Spain, visual acuity of 0.1 or less, or a visual field of 10 degrees or less, in the better eye with correction). Many legally blind people still have some sight.
Low vision
Vision loss that cannot be fully corrected with glasses, contact lenses, medication or surgery and that makes everyday tasks difficult, but where some useful residual vision remains.

M

Macula
The central part of the retina, responsible for detailed vision and much of our colour vision.

O

Optical low vision aid
A device with lenses that makes the image larger: hand-held or stand magnifiers, illuminated magnifiers, high-addition spectacles or telescopes. It should be chosen, and its use learned, with a professional.

P

Peripheral vision
The part of vision that sees to the sides, above and below while looking straight ahead. It is key to moving around without tripping. It is lost, for example, in advanced glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa.
Photophobia (light sensitivity)
Discomfort or pain caused by light, making it hard to see in bright conditions. Selective filters, peaked caps and dark mode on screens can help.

R

Rare disease
A disease that affects few people (in Europe, fewer than 5 in 10,000). Many inherited diseases of the retina and optic nerve are rare diseases.
Residual vision
The vision a person still has. With aids, good lighting and training it can be used much more effectively.
Retinitis pigmentosa
A group of inherited retinal diseases. It often starts with difficulty seeing at night and a gradual narrowing of the peripheral visual field.

S

Scotoma
An area of the visual field where vision is missing or reduced, surrounded by areas of preserved vision. It can be central (for example in AMD) or peripheral.
Screen magnifier
Software that enlarges part of a computer or phone screen. Operating systems include one (Windows Magnifier, Apple Zoom, Android Magnification) and there are dedicated products such as ZoomText.
Screen reader
Software that reads the screen content aloud (or shows it in braille). Examples include NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and TalkBack.
Sighted guide technique
A safe way of guiding a person with sight loss: they hold your arm just above the elbow while you walk half a step ahead and point out obstacles.

V

Visual acuity
The eye's ability to see fine detail. It is measured with charts of letters or symbols of decreasing size and recorded, for example, as a decimal value (1.0 is the usual reference), a Snellen fraction or logMAR.
Visual field
The whole area you can see while looking straight at one point, including peripheral (side) vision.
Visual rehabilitation
Training, guided by professionals, to make the best use of residual vision: reading techniques, eccentric viewing, using aids and strategies for daily life.

W

WCAG
The W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They define how to make websites usable by everyone, including people with visual or hearing impairments.
White cane
A cane used by people with visual impairment to detect obstacles and to let others know they see poorly. Many people with low vision use it only at certain times, for example at night.

Baixa visió en xarxa

An accessible, co-created digital platform that brings together, validates and humanises information on low vision and blindness for patients, families and the wider community, and professionals.
